description:
Join UmbraOnxy Team: NASA Space Apps 2026

We're building a research tool that reads NASA's microgravity combustion experiments (FLEX, SoFIE, ACME, SAFFIRE). It summarizes them, ranks them and answers questions about them, organized around the variables that control fire behavior: fuel, oxygen, pressure, flow, gravity, flame shape and extinction. The aim is to help people understand how fire behaves in space and what it means for crewed spacecraft and habitats.

What we've built so far

Document ingestion for NASA reports, theses and task books

AI extraction of structured experiment data, with an adjustable ranking system

A question box that answers from the sources, with cited passages

An animated Earth vs microgravity flame comparison

Tech stack

Backend: Python 3.12 and FastAPI

Data: Neon Postgres, with SQLite for local work

AI: Groq (gpt-oss-120b), with Ollama as an optional offline fallback

Frontend: plain JavaScript and Chart.js, with no framework

Hosting: AWS Lambda (SAM) and Cloudflare Pages

CI/CD: GitHub Actions

Who we're looking for

Backend and API developers

People who like working with data, retrieval and LLMs

Frontend and visualization builders

Anyone with an interest in physics, combustion or space science, even if you can't code

You don't need to be an expert in any of these. If you think you have it in you, join us.

To join: message [your name / contact link].
summary:
NASA holds decades of microgravity combustion data in its PSI database, but it is hard to find, compare and interpret. That matters as crews prepare for Moon and Mars habitats with higher-oxygen atmospheres, where materials burn more easily. The challenge asked for an AI-powered dashboard to rank and interpret these experiments for fire safety.

Flame in Freefall does this. It ranks 25 experiments (9 directly fire-safety relevant) using six adjustable factors, and checks each against six crew environments: ISS, spacecraft, Moon Base, rover, Mars base and spacesuit. Users can filter by fuel, hardware and focus (prevention, detection, suppression), compare experiments side by side, and see which variables each one covered. CSV/JSON export and a data-gap tracker support predictive modeling. Five control areas link experiments to next-generation equipment, and Earth applications such as water-mist extinguishers and smoke detectors are included.

Ask SI, our AI assistant, answers only from the indexed data and cites experiments, saying "I don't know" when the data is silent.

We state limits openly: no partial-gravity data exists yet, and Mars and spacecraft atmospheres are assumed.

Built with React, Python on AWS Lambda, Neon Postgres and Groq.

Team UmbraOnxy
details:
Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data

2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge · Team UmbraOnxy · Miguel Nyobole (mrviinccileroy), Lesego Mokoena (alondra_01)

  • Live site: https://flame-in-freefall.pages.dev/
  • Source code: https://github.com/Real-Vicinic/F-I-F/

1. Summary

Flame in Freefall is a web dashboard that ranks, compares and explains NASA's microgravity combustion experiments so that researchers and engineers can quickly see which ones matter for fire safety on the ISS, the Moon and Mars. It combines a transparent ranking engine, environment-fit analysis, a variable-coverage view, data export for modeling, and an AI assistant that answers only from the indexed data and cites its sources.

2. The problem

Fire is one of the most dangerous hazards in crewed spaceflight (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, the Mir fire). Without buoyancy, flames become spherical and diffusion-driven, so Earth-based fire safety assumptions do not simply carry over. The risk grows as habitats change: spacesuits use 100% oxygen at 4.3 psi, and Moon bases and pressurized rovers are expected to run at 30% or more oxygen at 10.2 psi or less, which is over 40% more oxygen than Earth air and makes materials far more flammable.

NASA's Physical Science Informatics (PSI) database holds decades of results from ISS combustion investigations, but the volume makes them hard to find, harder to compare and harder still to interpret. PSI also has no partial-gravity combustion data yet.

3. What the challenge asked

Build an interactive, SI-powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets PSI combustion investigations to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration. It should help users:

  1. Identify investigations most relevant to crew environments: spacecraft, space stations, Moon and Mars bases, pressurized rovers.
  2. Extract data that supports predictive modeling of flammability and fire scenarios.
  3. Highlight research that informs next-generation fire safety controls and equipment.
  4. Optionally, show applications of the research to fire safety on Earth.

It also suggested summarizing objectives, fuels, test conditions (oxygen, airflow), variables, sensors, and the similarities and differences between investigations.

4. What we built and how it answers each ask

Find the right investigations

  • 25 curated investigations (9 direct, 7 related, 9 indirect) covering BASS, BASS-II, FLEX, FLEX-2, Saffire-I/II/III, SAME, SAME-R, SPICE, SLICE, CFI, CFI-G, the ACME experiments (BRE, Flame Design, E-FIELD, CLD Flame, s-Flame), DAFT, DAFT-2, and ground-based university research.
  • Ranked Explorer with filters for fuel, hardware, relevance tier and focus (prevention, detection, suppression), plus text search.
  • Six adjustable ranking factors, blended live by sliders: fire relevance (0.25), evidence (0.20), variable coverage (0.20), actionability (0.15), atmosphere fit (0.10), data richness (0.10). A Re-rank button resets to defaults. Ranking runs in the browser, so changes are instant.
  • Environment fit for six crew environments: ISS-like (21% O₂, 14.7 psi), crewed spacecraft, Moon Base (30%, 10.2 psi), pressurized rover, Mars base, and spacesuit (100%, 4.3 psi). Each investigation is labeled confirmed, possible or unknown per environment, and values not given in the brief (spacecraft, Mars) are marked as assumed.
  • Oxygen tested vs habitat oxygen chart: for example BASS 17–21%, FLEX-2 10–40%, CFI-G up to 85%.

Compare and interpret

  • Detail page per investigation: objective, fuels, geometry, hardware, facility, oxygen, airflow, variables varied, sensors, what it informs, and similar investigations.
  • Side-by-side compare highlighting which fields are the same and which differ, plus shared tags.
  • Fire variable coverage matrix: 17 variables (fuel, form, geometry, O₂, diluent, pressure, ambient temperature, flow regime, flow velocity, gravity, ignition, flame shape, spread rate, peak temperature, extinction, limiting oxygen, products) showing what each investigation recorded or varied.
  • Fire physics reference explaining microgravity versus Earth flames (buoyancy, oxygen transport, low-speed flow, flammability limits, near-limit flames, heat transfer, cool flames, ventilation, partial gravity) with source links.

Data for predictive modeling

  • CSV and JSON export of investigations and of test conditions, filtered the same way as the table.
  • 21 test-condition rows (oxygen, pressure, airflow) imported from PSI and NASA sources.
  • Data-gap tracker showing which investigations still lack oxygen, pressure or airflow values and which need verifying in PSI.

Next-generation controls and equipment

Five control areas, each listing the investigations that inform it, ordered by score: material selection, atmosphere limits, smoke detection, suppression systems, and fire modeling.

Earth applications

Cards for water-mist extinguishers, particulate-and-species fire detectors, the shuttle-derived smoke detector, ultra-low-emission burners, firefighter air tanks and protective clothing, each linked to the related investigations. A history section covers Apollo 1, Apollo 13 and the Mir fire.

Ask SI: the AI assistant

A chat drawer that answers questions such as "Which experiments tested materials at 30%+ oxygen like the planned Moon Base?" or "How was fire suppression tested in microgravity?"

  • Retrieves matching text chunks with PostgreSQL full-text search, then sends only that context to Groq (Llama 3.3 70B).
  • Instructed to answer only from the context, cite investigations by name, and say "I don't know" when the data is silent.
  • Citations link back to each investigation's detail page.
  • Multiple Groq API keys rotate to avoid rate limits; if the model is unavailable, the assistant returns the matching indexed facts instead.

5. Architecture

Layer

Technology

Frontend

React + Vite, deployed to Cloudflare Pages

API

Python 3.12 on AWS Lambda behind API Gateway, deployed with AWS SAM

Database

Neon PostgreSQL: investigations, experiments, test conditions, text chunks with a GIN full-text index

AI

Groq (Llama 3.3 70B) with retrieval over the indexed chunks

CI/CD

GitHub Actions: backend, frontend and database workflows

API endpoints: investigations (list and detail), compare, coverage, equipment, hardware, environments, earth, meta, conditions, export, search, chat, health. The API also computes a 0–100 score with focus and environment boosts, used for exports and the compare view.

Data pipeline: investigation metadata is curated into a seed file and loaded into Neon with a seed script and numbered migrations; test conditions are imported from a CSV; a Playwright-based GitHub Actions workflow can harvest PSI investigation pages for verification.

Quality: pytest suites for the scoring logic and the API, plus an end-to-end smoke test.

6. Honest limits

  • PSI has no partial-gravity combustion data yet; the dashboard says so and points to LUCI and FM2 as expected sources, with E-FIELD Flames as an electric-field analogue.
  • Mars and crewed-spacecraft atmospheres are not in the challenge brief, so they are assumed and labeled as such.
  • No test reaches 100% oxygen spacesuit conditions; CFI-G (up to 85%) is the closest bound.
  • ISS-condition findings may not transfer to exploration atmospheres.
  • The dashboard ranks curated metadata; raw measurements remain in PSI.
  • Rocket and propellant combustion is out of scope, as in the challenge.

7. Next steps

  • Add Moon-gravity results from LUCI and FM2 as they are published in PSI.
  • Ingest raw measurements to support direct predictive modeling.
  • Refine Mars and spacecraft atmospheres with official NASA values.
  • Expand test-condition coverage and verify flagged records.

8. Team

UmbraOnxy: Miguel Nyobole (mrviinccileroy) and Lesego Mokoena (alondra_01).
